title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, CFO Colette Kress named interim chief
subtitle: The board accepted Huang's resignation on November 12 after scandal reporting and a late-night meeting the night before. Kress keeps the CFO role while a formal search begins, with earnings due November 17.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia announced on Thursday, November 12 that Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive, and member of the board, effective immediately. The board named CFO Colette Kress, who has held the finance job since 2013, as interim chief executive while retaining her CFO duties and while a formal successor search begins across internal and external candidates. The resignation followed a late-night board meeting the previous evening and reporting over the preceding week that tied Huang to two extramarital relationships — one with a businesswoman alleged by outside investigators to be a Chinese intelligence operative, and a second with an Nvidia executive who reported up his management chain. Huang acknowledged in an internal note to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia shares fell more than 13 percent in early Thursday trading before paring losses.

Kress is the operational choice, not a strategic one. She has run the finance function through the company's rise from a 15 billion dollar graphics vendor to the center of the global AI buildout, and the board picked continuity over disruption with earnings arriving on November 17. The permanent succession question is harder. Ian Buck, who runs the data-center business, is the most frequently named internal candidate in the reporting, but no sitting Nvidia executive has Huang's product and partnership range. Nvidia's roadmap commitments — Rubin and successor accelerators, the Isaac robotics stack, sovereign-AI contracts in the Gulf, Europe and the UK — were in large part negotiated personally by Huang, and the board has to decide whether to promote an operator who can execute what exists or to recruit an outside strategist who can set the next decade.

The industry effect is already visible in the capex conversation. Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon have each pointed to trillion-dollar AI infrastructure plans that lean heavily on Nvidia silicon; those plans do not change this week, but the pace of hyperscaler diversification toward Google TPUs, Amazon's Trainium line, and in-house accelerators will almost certainly pick up. Washington has an interest in the succession too: a large share of Nvidia's recent revenue growth has come through US-blessed deals with allied governments, and the counter-intelligence concern that helped force Huang out means the next permanent CEO will be vetted as a national-security figure as much as a corporate one. The November 17 earnings call is now also a governance update, which is not how Nvidia likes to run its quarters.

A takeaway for learners: in a company with a founder at the center, the handoff is the job. Watch how Nvidia communicates about Kress's mandate over the next month — whether she is framed as a steady operator or as a contender for the permanent seat — because that signal tells you whether the board wants continuity or a reset. If you are early in your career and work in an org where one person holds the vision, the roadmap, and the external relationships, assume that person's succession plan is a risk you carry. Read the proxy statement, read the 10-K's risk factors, and keep an eye on who speaks on earnings calls. Concentration of judgment is a tailwind until the day it isn't.
